articles.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
articles.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.
articles.content:
Archaeologists from La Trobe University have described 18 newly published hominin fossils from South Africa, including a second skull fragment belonging to Homo erectus. The discovery adds stronger evidence that the species was present in southern Africa 2.0 million years ago, about 200,000 years earlier than traditionally believed.

The fossil collection also includes remains of P. robustus. Those specimens suggest the species was undergoing gradual evolutionary changes as it adapted to shifting environmental and climatic conditions.

Fossils From South Africa's Cradle of Humankind

The fossils come from Drimolen Main Quarry in South Africa's 'Cradle of Humankind,' one of the world's richest sites for remains of ancient human relatives. Although the quarry was discovered in 1992 and excavated through 2019, many of the fossils recovered there had never been formally described and remained largely unknown to science.

Researchers from La Trobe, working with colleagues in South Africa and the United States, have now analyzed and described another 18 fossils from the site. The remains have been assigned to Homo erectus and P. robustus.

In research published in Annals of Human Biology, the team reports the first known adult Homo erectus fossil from Drimolen. The specimen is about 2 million years old, making it roughly 200,000 years older than adult Homo erectus fossils discovered elsewhere, including specimens from Dmanisi in Georgia that date to about 1.8 million years ago.

"Homo erectus is the first species of hominin that researchers broadly agree fits within our own genus Homo and is likely directly ancestral to us. Drimolen preserves evidence for the first appearance of this species 2 million years ago; however, the original fossil, DNH 134, belonged to a child aged between two and four, and there was uncertainty about what the adult version may have looked like," lead researcher Dr. Jesse Martin said.

"This paper publishes a new adult fossil attributed to Homo erectus, DNH 127, providing further confirmation that this species first appeared in southern Africa 2 million years ago."

Two Human Relatives Took Different Evolutionary Paths

The newly described fossils also provide evidence that P. robustus changed over time. Between about 2 million and 1.8 million years ago, the species developed larger teeth and more powerful chewing muscles.

According to Dr. Martin, the contrast with Homo erectus is striking. While Homo erectus was developing a larger brain and smaller molar teeth, possibly as a result of eating more meat, P. robustus retained a brain only slightly larger than that of chimpanzees. At the same time, it evolved enormous molars suited to grinding and crushing tough, hard foods, functioning much like a mortar and pestle.

"These two human species shared the same landscape and are both preserved in Drimolen cave. While we know that Homo erectus and the lineage leading to us was ultimately the successful one, 2 million years ago P. robustus outnumbered Homo erectus at Drimolen by more than 10 to one. During this time period, it was our ancestors that looked like the outside long-odds chance to survive," Dr. Martin said.

Fossils Reveal Evolution in Action

The Drimolen fossils also help researchers compare P. robustus populations separated by about 200,000 years.

"This paper confirms that the P. robustus fossils from the 2-million-year-old Drimolen Cave are slightly but importantly different from the P. Robustus fossils at the 1.8-million-year-old Swartkrans cave.

"During this 200,000-year period, P. robustus teeth became even larger, and so did the muscles associated with chewing. Hominin fossils are so rare that generally the differences between them are huge, and researchers are left to make educated guesses regarding what existed in the missing parts of the fossil record.

"However, the large number of fossils from Drimolen, some of which are published in this paper, allow an unprecedented insight into the micro-evolutionary changes that shaped human ancestors.

Dr. Martin said researchers had already recognized that the Drimolen population of P. robustus was distinctive enough to receive a separate subspecies designation, P. Robustus ukusa. The newly described fossils provide additional support for that formal classification.

The research involved scientists from the Palaeoscience Labs, Department of Archaeology and History, La Trobe University, Palaeo-Research Institute, University of Johannesburg, Evolutionary Studies Institute, University of the Witwatersrand, and Department of Anthropology, Washington University.

articles.personality_title: New fossils show Homo erectus lived 200,000 years earlier in South Africa
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists study fossils to learn about early human ancestors and how they evolved. South Africa’s Cradle of Humankind is a key place where many ancient bones have been found.

**What happened** – Researchers found and studied 18 fossils from Drimolen Cave in South Africa. Among them was a skull piece from an adult Homo erectus dated about 2 million years old. This is 200,000 years older than other known adult fossils of this species. They also found fossils of Paranthropus robustus, a different human relative, showing it was changing over time.

**Impact** – This discovery changes what we thought about when Homo erectus first lived. It shows that this important ancestor appeared earlier than believed, giving scientists a better timeline of human evolution. It also reveals how two different species living together adapted in different ways—Homo erectus developing bigger brains, while P. robustus grew bigger teeth and stronger chewing muscles.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue studying these fossils and others from the area to learn more about how early humans lived and evolved. They may also look for more fossils to fill gaps in the timeline and understand how ancient environments affected these species.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Fossils from South Africa prove Homo erectus lived 200,000 years earlier than thought, reshaping our understanding of early human evolution.
articles.personality_title_fr: De nouveaux fossiles montrent que Homo erectus vivait 200 000 ans plus tôt en Afrique du Sud
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques étudient les fossiles pour mieux comprendre les premiers ancêtres humains et leur évolution. Le berceau de l’humanité en Afrique du Sud est un site important où de nombreux os anciens ont été découverts.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs ont analysé 18 fossiles de la grotte Drimolen en Afrique du Sud. Parmi eux, un fragment de crâne d’un Homo erectus adulte daté d’environ 2 millions d’années. C’est 200 000 ans plus ancien que les autres fossiles adultes connus. Ils ont aussi trouvé des fossiles de Paranthropus robustus, un autre parent humain, montrant son évolution.

**Impact** – Cette découverte change nos idées sur l’apparition d’Homo erectus. Elle montre que cet ancêtre important est apparu plus tôt que prévu, améliorant la chronologie de l’évolution humaine. Elle révèle aussi comment deux espèces différentes vivant ensemble ont évolué différemment : Homo erectus avec un cerveau plus grand, P. robustus avec des dents et des muscles de mastication plus puissants.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont continuer à étudier ces fossiles et d’autres dans la région pour mieux comprendre la vie et l’évolution des premiers humains. Ils chercheront aussi d’autres fossiles pour combler les lacunes dans la chronologie et comprendre comment les anciens environnements ont influencé ces espèces.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des fossiles d’Afrique du Sud prouvent qu’Homo erectus vivait 200 000 ans plus tôt que prévu, modifiant notre compréhension de l’évolution humaine.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevos fósiles muestran que Homo erectus vivió 200,000 años antes en Sudáfrica
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos estudian fósiles para entender a los primeros antepasados humanos y cómo evolucionaron. La Cuna de la Humanidad en Sudáfrica es un lugar clave donde se han encontrado muchos huesos antiguos.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores analizaron 18 fósiles de la Cueva Drimolen en Sudáfrica. Entre ellos había un fragmento de cráneo de un Homo erectus adulto con una antigüedad de unos 2 millones de años. Esto es 200,000 años más antiguo que otros fósiles adultos conocidos. También encontraron fósiles de Paranthropus robustus, otro pariente humano que estaba cambiando con el tiempo.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo cambia lo que se creía sobre cuándo apareció Homo erectus. Muestra que este importante ancestro vivió antes de lo pensado, mejorando la línea de tiempo de la evolución humana. También revela cómo dos especies diferentes que vivían juntas se adaptaron de manera distinta: Homo erectus con cerebros más grandes, y P. robustus con dientes y músculos de masticación más fuertes.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán estudiando estos y otros fósiles para aprender más sobre cómo vivían y evolucionaban los primeros humanos. Buscarán más fósiles para llenar los espacios en la línea de tiempo y entender cómo los ambientes antiguos afectaron a estas especies.

**Resumen en una frase** – Fósiles de Sudáfrica muestran que Homo erectus vivió 200,000 años antes de lo pensado, cambiando nuestra comprensión de la evolución humana.
articles.image_prompt: A detailed, warm-toned painting of two ancient hominin skull fragments—one larger and more refined representing adult Homo erectus, and one with large molars symbolizing P. robustus—resting gently on layered sediment strata illuminated by soft natural light, set within the rocky entrance of Drimolen Cave in South Africa’s Cradle of Humankind.
